questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In LCR series circuit at resonance
options: the current and voltage are in phase.
questions.solution:
In an LCR series circuit, the impedance is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

At resonance, the inductive reactance is equal to the capacitive reactance, i.e., $X_L = X_C$.

Substituting this in the impedance formula, we get $Z = R$. This is the minimum possible impedance, which results in maximum current.

The phase difference $\phi$ between the voltage and current is given by $\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

Since $X_L = X_C$, $\tan \phi = 0 \Rightarrow \phi = 0$.

Thus, the current and voltage are in phase.

Answer: the current and voltage are in phase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The LC series resonant circuit produces a resonant frequency '$f$'. If L is tripled and 'C' is increased by 3C, the resonant frequency will be
questions.solution:
The resonant frequency of an LC series circuit is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

Given that the inductance $L$ is tripled, the new inductance is $L' = 3L$.

The capacitance $C$ is increased by $3C$, so the new capacitance is $C' = C + 3C = 4C$.

The new resonant frequency $f'$ is given by:

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L'C'}}$

Substituting the values of $L'$ and $C'$:

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(3L)(4C)}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{12LC}}$

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \left( \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \right)$

$f' = \dfrac{f}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{f}{2\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistor '$R$' inductance '$L$' and capacitance '$C$' are connected in series with an a.c. source. When 'L' is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between voltage and current in the circuit is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. If instead, C is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. The power factor of the circuit is
questions.solution:
When $L$ is removed, the circuit becomes an $RC$ circuit. The phase difference is $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_C}{R} \Rightarrow \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{X_C}{R} \Rightarrow X_C = R\sqrt{3}$

When $C$ is removed, the circuit becomes an $RL$ circuit. The phase difference is again $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L}{R} \Rightarrow \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{X_L}{R} \Rightarrow X_L = R\sqrt{3}$

In the series $RLC$ circuit, the net reactance is $X = X_L - X_C$.

Since $X_L = X_C = R\sqrt{3}$, we have $X = 0$.

The impedance of the circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R$.

The power factor of the circuit is $\cos \phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{R}{R} = 1$.

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inductor of inductance $2\ \mu\text{H}$ is connected in series with a resistance, a variable capacitor and an a.c. source of 10 kHz. The value of capacitance for which maximum current is drawn in to the circuit is $\dfrac{1}{x}\ \text{F}$, where the value of x is (Take $\pi^2 = 10$)
questions.solution:
Maximum current is drawn in a series LCR circuit at resonance.

At resonance, the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance, so $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.

$C = \dfrac{1}{\omega^2 L} = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi f)^2 L}$

Given $L = 2\ \mu\text{H} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{H}$ and $f = 10\ \text{kHz} = 10^4\ \text{Hz}$.

$C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2 f^2 L}$

Substituting the values and using $\pi^2 = 10$:

$C = \dfrac{1}{4 \times 10 \times (10^4)^2 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{40 \times 10^8 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{80 \times 10^2} = \dfrac{1}{8000}\ \text{F}$

Comparing with $C = \dfrac{1}{x}\ \text{F}$, we get $x = 8000$.

Answer: $8000$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Series LCR circuit containing an a.c. source of 100V has a inductor and a capacitor of reactance $24\ \Omega$ and $16\ \Omega$ respectively. If a resistance of $6\ \Omega$ is connected in series, then the potential difference across the series combination of inductor and capacitor only is
questions.solution:
Given $V = 100\text{V}$, $X_L = 24\ \Omega$, $X_C = 16\ \Omega$, and $R = 6\ \Omega$.

The net reactance of the circuit is $X = X_L - X_C = 24 - 16 = 8\ \Omega$.

The impedance of the series LCR circuit is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

Substituting the values, $Z = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\ \Omega$.

The rms current in the circuit is $I = \dfrac{V}{Z} = \dfrac{100}{10} = 10\text{A}$.

The potential difference across the series combination of the inductor and capacitor is $V_{LC} = I \times |X_L - X_C|$.

$V_{LC} = 10 \times 8 = 80\text{V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Alternating current of peak value $\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$ A flows through the primary coil of a transformer. The coefficient of mutual inductance between primary and secondary coils is 1H. The peak value of induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil is
(Frequency of a.c. = 50 Hz)
questions.solution:
The current in the primary coil is $I = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$.

The induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil is given by $e = -M \dfrac{dI}{dt}$.

$e = -M \dfrac{d}{dt} (I_0 \sin(\omega t)) = -M I_0 \omega \cos(\omega t)$

The peak value of the induced e.m.f. is $e_0 = M I_0 \omega$.

Given $M = 1$ H, $I_0 = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$ A, and $f = 50$ Hz.

The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi$ rad/s.

Substituting the values, we get:

$e_0 = 1 \times \left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right) \times 100\pi = 200$ V.

Answer: $200\text{V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A step down transformer has turns ratio 20:1. If 8V are applied across $0.4\ \Omega$ secondary then the primary current will be
questions.solution:
Given turns ratio $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s} = 20$

Secondary voltage $V_s = 8$ V

Secondary resistance $R_s = 0.4\ \Omega$

Secondary current $I_s = \dfrac{V_s}{R_s} = \dfrac{8}{0.4} = 20$ A

For an ideal transformer, $\dfrac{I_p}{I_s} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$

$I_p = I_s \times \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 20 \times \dfrac{1}{20} = 1$ A

Answer: $1$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An alternating e.m.f. is given by $e = e_0 \sin\omega t$. In what time the e.m.f. will have half its maximum value, if 'e' Starts from zero?
questions.solution:
Given alternating e.m.f. is $e = e_0 \sin\omega t$.

The maximum value of e.m.f. is $e_0$.

We need to find the time $t$ when $e = \dfrac{e_0}{2}$.

Substituting $e = \dfrac{e_0}{2}$ in the given equation:

$\dfrac{e_0}{2} = e_0 \sin\omega t$

$\sin\omega t = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The smallest positive value for $\omega t$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

Substituting $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$:

$\dfrac{2\pi}{T} t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$t = \dfrac{T}{12}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\text{T}}{12}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With gradual increase in frequency of an a.c. supply, the impedance of an LCR series circuit
options: first decreases, becomes minimum and then increases
questions.solution:
The impedance of an LCR series circuit is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

where $X_L = 2\pi f L$ and $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$.

At low frequencies, $X_C > X_L$, so the impedance is high.

As the frequency $f$ increases, $X_C$ decreases and $X_L$ increases, which reduces the magnitude of $(X_L - X_C)$. Thus, the impedance decreases.

At the resonant frequency $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, $X_L = X_C$, and the impedance becomes minimum, $Z = R$.

With a further increase in frequency, $X_L > X_C$, and the magnitude of $(X_L - X_C)$ increases, causing the impedance to increase.

Therefore, the impedance first decreases, becomes minimum, and then increases.

Answer: first decreases, becomes minimum and then increases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a capacitor is connected in series LR circuit, the alternating current flowing in the circuit
questions.solution:
The impedance of a series LR circuit is given by $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

When a capacitor is connected in series with the LR circuit, it becomes an LCR circuit. The new impedance is given by $Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

The net reactance of the circuit changes from $X_L$ to $|X_L - X_C|$. Since the capacitive reactance $X_C$ opposes the inductive reactance $X_L$, the net reactance generally decreases.

As a result, the overall impedance of the circuit decreases ($Z_2 \lt Z_1$).

Since the alternating current is inversely proportional to the impedance ($I = \dfrac{V}{Z}$), a decrease in impedance leads to an increase in the current flowing through the circuit.

Answer: increases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an LCR series circuit, at resonance,
options: the current and voltage are in phase
questions.solution:
In an LCR series circuit, the impedance is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

At resonance, the inductive reactance is equal to the capacitive reactance, i.e., $X_L = X_C$.

Substituting this in the impedance formula, we get $Z = R$, which is the minimum impedance.

The phase difference $\phi$ between the voltage and current is given by $\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

Since $X_L = X_C$, $\tan \phi = 0 \Rightarrow \phi = 0$.

Therefore, the current and voltage are in phase.

Answer: the current and voltage are in phase

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series resonant circuit consists of an inductor 'L' and capacitor 'C' which produces resonant frequency 'f'. If 'L' is increased by '2L' and 'C' is changed to '9C' the resonant frequency will be
questions.solution:
The resonant frequency of a series L-C circuit is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$

Given that the inductance is increased by $2L$, the new inductance is:

$L' = L + 2L = 3L$

The capacitance is changed to $9C$, so the new capacitance is:

$C' = 9C$

The new resonant frequency $f'$ is:

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L'C'}}$

Substituting the values of $L'$ and $C'$:

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(3L)(9C)}}$

$f' = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{27LC}}$

$f' = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} \left( \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \right)$

$f' = \dfrac{f}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{f}{3\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric lamp connected in series with a capacitor and an a.c source is glowing with certain brightness. On reducing the frequency of source the brightness of the lamp
questions.solution:
The impedance of the series RC circuit is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}$, where $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$.

When the frequency $f$ of the AC source is reduced, the capacitive reactance $X_C$ increases.

As a result, the total impedance $Z$ of the circuit increases.

The current in the circuit is $I = \dfrac{V}{Z}$. Since $Z$ increases, the current $I$ decreases.

The brightness of the lamp is proportional to the power dissipated, $P = I^2 R$. With a decrease in current, the power dissipated decreases, and hence the brightness of the lamp is reduced.

Answer: is reduced

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil has inductive reactance $3$ H. The ratio of its reactance when it is first connected to an a.c. source and then to d.c. source is
questions.solution:
The inductive reactance of a coil is given by $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L$, where $f$ is the frequency of the source.

For an a.c. source, the frequency $f > 0$, so the inductive reactance $X_{L(ac)}$ has a finite non-zero value.

For a d.c. source, the frequency $f = 0$, so the inductive reactance $X_{L(dc)} = 0$.

The ratio of the reactance when connected to an a.c. source to that when connected to a d.c. source is:

$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{X_{L(ac)}}{X_{L(dc)}} = \dfrac{\omega L}{0} = \infty$

Thus, the ratio is infinite.

Answer: infinite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the frequency for which a $10\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor has a reactance of $2 \times 10^{-3}\,\Omega$.
questions.solution:
The capacitive reactance is given by the formula:

$X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$

Rearranging for frequency $f$:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi X_C C}$

Substituting the given values $X_C = 2 \times 10^{-3} \, \Omega$ and $C = 10 \, \mu\text{F} = 10 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{F}$:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times (2 \times 10^{-3}) \times (10 \times 10^{-6})}$

$f = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \times 10^{-8}}$

$f = \dfrac{10^8}{4\pi}$

$f = \dfrac{100 \times 10^6}{4\pi}$

$f = \dfrac{25}{\pi} \times 10^6 \, \text{Hz}$

$f = \dfrac{25}{\pi} \, \text{MHz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected to an a.c. source of $220$ V, $50$ Hz. The circuit contains a resistance $R = 80\,\Omega$, an inductor of inductive reactance $70\,\Omega$ and capacitor of capacitive reactance $130\,\Omega$. The power factor of the circuit is $\dfrac{x}{10}$. The value of x is
questions.solution:
The impedance of the series LCR circuit is given by

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$Z = \sqrt{80^2 + (130 - 70)^2}$

$Z = \sqrt{80^2 + 60^2}$

$Z = \sqrt{6400 + 3600} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\,\Omega$

The power factor of the circuit is

$\cos \phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}$

$\cos \phi = \dfrac{80}{100} = \dfrac{8}{10}$

Comparing this with $\dfrac{x}{10}$, we get $x = 8$.

Answer: $8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a series LR circuit with $X_L = R$. Power factor is $P_1$. If a capacitor of capacitance $C$ with $X_c = X_L$ is added to the circuit the power factor becomes $P_2$. The ratio of $P_1$ to $P_2$ will be :
questions.solution:
For the initial series LR circuit, the impedance is $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

Given $X_L = R$, we have $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + R^2} = \sqrt{2}R$.

The power factor $P_1 = \dfrac{R}{Z_1} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}R} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

When a capacitor with $X_C = X_L$ is added in series, the new impedance is $Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

Since $X_C = X_L$, the circuit is in resonance and $Z_2 = R$.

The new power factor $P_2 = \dfrac{R}{Z_2} = \dfrac{R}{R} = 1$.

The ratio of $P_1$ to $P_2$ is $\dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Thus, $P_1 : P_2 = 1 : \sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inductor of $0.5$ mH, a capacitor of $20\mu$ F and resistance $20\,\Omega$ are connected in series with a $220$ V ac source. If the current is in phase with the emf, the amplitude of current of the circuit is $[x]^{1/2}$ A. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Since the current is in phase with the emf, the circuit is in resonance.

At resonance, the impedance of the circuit is equal to its resistance.

$Z = R = 20\,\Omega$

The rms current in the circuit is given by:

$I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{220}{20} = 11$ A

The amplitude (peak value) of the current is:

$I_{0} = \sqrt{2} I_{rms} = 11\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{242}$ A

Given that the amplitude of the current is $\sqrt{x} A, we have:

\sqrt{x} = \sqrt{242} \Rightarrow x = 242$

Answer: $242$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In the circuit shown, the ratio of the quality factor and the band width is
(Given: band width = R/L)
questions.solution:
The quality factor $Q$ of a series LCR circuit is given by:

$Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R}$

where $\omega_0$ is the resonant angular frequency, $\omega_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{LC}}$.

The bandwidth is given as $\Delta \omega = \dfrac{R}{L}$.

The ratio of the quality factor to the bandwidth is:

$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{Q}{\Delta \omega} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R}}{\dfrac{R}{L}} = \omega_0 \dfrac{L^2}{R^2}$

Substituting $\omega_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{LC}}$, we get:

$\text{Ratio} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{LC}} \dfrac{L^2}{R^2}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{LC}}\dfrac{L^2}{R^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resistor of 100 $\Omega$, inductor of self inductance $\left(\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\right)$ H and a capacitor of unknown capacity are connected in series to an a.c. source of 200 V and 50 Hz. When the current and voltage are in phase, the value of capacity is
questions.solution:
When current and voltage are in phase, the circuit is in resonance.

$X_L = X_C$

$\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{\omega^2 L}$

Given $f = 50$ Hz, $\omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi$ rad/s and $L = \dfrac{4}{\pi^2}$ H.

Substituting the values:

$C = \dfrac{1}{(100\pi)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\right)}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{10000\pi^2 \times \dfrac{4}{\pi^2}}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{40000}$ F

$C = 25 \times 10^{-6}$ F $= 25 \ \mu F$

Answer: $25 \ \mu F$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An alternating e.m.f. is given by $e = e_0 \sin \omega t$. In what time the e.m.f. will have half its maximum value, if 'e' starts from zero? (\sin 30^{}^{\circ} = 0.5$)$
questions.solution:
Given $e = e_0 \sin \omega t$

The maximum value of e.m.f. is $e_0$. The time $t$ when the e.m.f. reaches half of its maximum value is given by $e = \dfrac{e_0}{2}$.

Substituting $e = \dfrac{e_0}{2}$ in the given equation:

$\dfrac{e_0}{2} = e_0 \sin \omega t$

$\sin \omega t = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

Substituting $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$:

$\dfrac{2\pi}{T} t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$t = \dfrac{T}{12}$

Answer: $\dfrac{T}{12}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR resonant circuit, R=800 $\Omega$, C = 2 $\mu$ F and voltage across resistance is 200 V. The angular frequency is 250 rad/s. At resonance the voltage across the capacitance is
questions.solution:
At resonance, the current in the circuit is determined by the resistance and the voltage across it.

$I = \dfrac{V_R}{R}$

Substituting the given values:

$I = \dfrac{200}{800} = 0.25$ A

The capacitive reactance is given by:

$X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$

Substituting the given values:

$X_C = \dfrac{1}{250 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{10^6}{500} = 2000 \, \Omega$

The voltage across the capacitance is:

$V_C = I X_C$

$V_C = 0.25 \times 2000 = 500$ V

Answer: $500$ V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR circuit C = 2 uF, L=1 mH and R= 10 $\Omega$. What is the ratio of energies stored in the capacitor and inductor when maximum current flows through circuit?
questions.solution:
For a series LCR circuit undergoing free oscillations, the voltage equation is given by:

$V_L + V_R + V_C = 0$

$L \dfrac{di}{dt} + iR + V_C = 0$

When the current $i$ in the circuit is maximum, its rate of change is zero, i.e., $\dfrac{di}{dt} = 0$.

Substituting this into the voltage equation, we get:

$0 + i_\maxR + V_C = 0 \Rightarrow V_C = -i_\maxR$

The energy stored in the capacitor at this instant is:

$U_C = \dfrac{1}{2} C V_C^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} C (i_\maxR)^2$

The energy stored in the inductor at the same instant is:

$U_L = \dfrac{1}{2} L i_\max^2$

The ratio of the energy stored in the capacitor to that in the inductor is:

$\dfrac{U_C}{U_L} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} C i_\max^2 R^2}{\dfrac{1}{2} L i_\max^2} = \dfrac{CR^2}{L}$

Given values are:

$C = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$

$R = 10 \Omega$

$L = 10^{-3} \text{ H}$

Substituting the given values into the ratio:

$\dfrac{U_C}{U_L} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times (10)^2}{10^{-3}}$

$\dfrac{U_C}{U_L} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{10^{-3}} = 0.2$

Thus, the ratio of energies is $0.2 : 1$.

Answer: $0.2 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Alternating current of peak value $\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$ A flows through the primary coil of a transformer. The coefficient of mutual inductance between primary and secondary coils is $1$ H. The peak em.f. induced in secondary coil is (Frequency of a. c. is $50$ Hz)
questions.solution:
The alternating current in the primary coil is given by $I_p = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, where $I_0$ is the peak current and $\omega = 2\pi f$.

The induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil is given by Faraday's law of induction:

$e_s = -M \dfrac{dI_p}{dt}$

$e_s = -M \dfrac{d}{dt} (I_0 \sin(\omega t))$

$e_s = -M I_0 \omega \cos(\omega t)$

The peak e.m.f. induced in the secondary coil is the maximum value of $e_s$, which is:

$E_0 = M I_0 \omega$

Given values are:

$M = 1$ H

$I_0 = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$ A

$f = 50$ Hz $\Rightarrow \omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi$ rad/s

Substituting these values into the equation for peak e.m.f.:

$E_0 = 1 \times \left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right) \times 100\pi$

$E_0 = 200$ V

Answer: $200$ V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal transformer converts $220$V a.c. to $3.3$ KV a.c. to transmit a power of $4.4$ KW. If primary coil has $600$ turns then alternating current in the secondary coil is
questions.solution:
For an ideal transformer, the input power is equal to the output power.

$P_{out} = P_{in} = 4.4 \text{ kW} = 4400 \text{ W}$

The output power is given by $P_{out} = V_s I_s$

$4400 = 3300 \times I_s$

$I_s = \dfrac{4400}{3300} = \dfrac{4}{3} \text{ A}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{3}$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR circuit, resistance is $18\ \Omega$ and impedance $33\ \Omega$. An r.m.s. Voltage of $220$ V is applied across the circuit. The true power consumed in a c. circuit is
questions.solution:
The true power consumed in an AC circuit is given by the formula:

$P = I_{rms}^2 R$

The rms current in the circuit is:

$I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}$

Substituting the given values $V_{rms} = 220$ V and $Z = 33\ \Omega$:

$I_{rms} = \dfrac{220}{33} = \dfrac{20}{3}$ A

Now, substituting $I_{rms}$ and $R = 18\ \Omega$ into the power formula:

$P = \left(\dfrac{20}{3}\right)^2 \times 18$

$P = \dfrac{400}{9} \times 18$

$P = 800$ W

Answer: $800$ W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In an a.c. circuit containing L, C and R in series, the ratio of apparent power to the true power is
(Z= impedance of the circuit and R= resistance )
questions.solution:
Apparent power is given by $P_{app} = V_{rms} I_{rms}$

True power is given by $P_{true} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \phi$

The ratio of apparent power to true power is $\dfrac{P_{app}}{P_{true}} = \dfrac{V_{rms} I_{rms}}{V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \phi} = \dfrac{1}{\cos \phi}$

In a series LCR circuit, the power factor is $\cos \phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}$

Substituting this value, the ratio becomes $\dfrac{Z}{R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{Z}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light bulb connected in series with a capacitor and an a.c.source is glowing with certain brightness. On reducing the value of capacitance and frequency respectively, the brightness of the bulb
questions.solution:
The brightness of the bulb depends on the current flowing through it, which is given by $I = \dfrac{V}{Z}$.

The impedance of the series RC circuit is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}$, where $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C}$.

When the capacitance $C$ is reduced, the capacitive reactance $X_C$ increases. This increases the total impedance $Z$ of the circuit, which in turn reduces the current $I$. Consequently, the brightness of the bulb is reduced.

Similarly, when the frequency $f$ of the AC source is reduced, the capacitive reactance $X_C$ increases. This again increases the impedance $Z$ and reduces the current $I$. Thus, the brightness of the bulb is reduced.

Therefore, in both cases, the brightness of the bulb is reduced.

Answer: is reduced, is reduced

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the circuit shown below, the ac source has voltage $V = 30 \cos(\omega t)$ volt with $\omega = 2000$ rad/s. What will be the amplitude of the current?
questions.solution:
From the given circuit, the parameters are:
Amplitude of voltage, $V_m = 30$ V
Angular frequency, $\omega = 2000$ rad/s
Total resistance, $R = 6 + 4 = 10\ \Omega$
Inductance, $L = 5 \times 10^{-3}$ H
Capacitance, $C = 50 \times 10^{-6}$ F

The inductive reactance is:
$X_L = \omega L = 2000 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 10\ \Omega$

The capacitive reactance is:
$X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2000 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\ \Omega$

The total impedance of the circuit is:
$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

Substituting the values:
$Z = \sqrt{10^2 + (10 - 10)^2} = 10\ \Omega$

The amplitude of the current is:
$I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{Z} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ A

Answer: $3$ A
questions.question: In the circuit shown below, the ac source has voltage $V = 30 \cos(\omega t)$ volt with $\omega = 2000$ rad/s. What will be the amplitude of the current?
questions.explanation:
From the given circuit, the parameters are:
Amplitude of voltage, $V_m = 30$ V
Angular frequency, $\omega = 2000$ rad/s
Total resistance, $R = 6 + 4 = 10\ \Omega$
Inductance, $L = 5 \times 10^{-3}$ H
Capacitance, $C = 50 \times 10^{-6}$ F

The inductive reactance is:
$X_L = \omega L = 2000 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 10\ \Omega$

The capacitive reactance is:
$X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2000 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\ \Omega$

The total impedance of the circuit is:
$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

Substituting the values:
$Z = \sqrt{10^2 + (10 - 10)^2} = 10\ \Omega$

The amplitude of the current is:
$I_m = \dfrac{V_m}{Z} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ A

Answer: $3$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an AC circuit $E = 50 \sin(500 t)$, $I = 600 \sin\left(500 t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) mA$. What is the power dissipated in the circuit? [\cos 60^{}^{\circ} = 0.5$]$
questions.solution:
The average power dissipated in an AC circuit is given by $P = E_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \phi$.

From the given equations, the peak voltage is $E_0 = 50$ V and the peak current is $I_0 = 600$ mA $= 0.6$ A.

The phase difference between the voltage and current is $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 60^{}^{\circ}$.

Using the relations $E_{rms} = \dfrac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$, the power is:

$P = \dfrac{E_0 I_0}{2} \cos \phi$

Substituting the values:

$P = \dfrac{50 \times 0.6}{2} \cos 60^{}^{\circ}$

$P = \dfrac{30}{2} \times 0.5 = 15 \times 0.5 = 7.5$ W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inductor of reactance $100\Omega$, a capacitor of reactance $50\Omega$, and a resistor of resistance $50\Omega$ are connected in series with an AC source of $10$ V, $50$ Hz. Average power dissipated by the circuit is ____
questions.solution:
Given $X_L = 100\Omega$, $X_C = 50\Omega$, and $R = 50\Omega$.

The impedance of the series LCR circuit is given by:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

$Z = \sqrt{50^2 + (100 - 50)^2} = \sqrt{50^2 + 50^2} = 50\sqrt{2}\Omega$

The RMS current in the circuit is:

$I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{10}{50\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}$ A

The average power dissipated in the circuit is:

$P_{avg} = I_{rms}^2 R$

$P_{avg} = \left(\dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \times 50 = \dfrac{1}{50} \times 50 = 1$ W

Answer: $1$ W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an LC circuit, angular frequency at resonance is $\omega$. The new angular frequency when inductance is made four times and capacitance is made eight times is
questions.solution:
The angular frequency at resonance for an LC circuit is given by $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

When both inductance and capacitance are increased by factors of 4 and 8 respectively, the new inductance becomes $L' = 4L$ and the new capacitance $C' = 8C$. The new angular frequency is therefore

$\omega' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4L)(8C)}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{32LC}} = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\sqrt{LC}}$.

Recognizing that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \omega$, we substitute to obtain

$\omega' = \frac{\omega}{4\sqrt{2}}$.

The new angular frequency is thus reduced by a factor of $4\sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The value of alternating e.m.f. (E) in the given circuit is
questions.solution:
A series LCR circuit has the voltage across the inductor as $V_L = 20\text{ V}$, across the capacitor as $V_C = 50\text{ V}$, and across the resistor as $V_R = 40\text{ V}$.

The resistor voltage is in phase with the current, while the inductor voltage leads by $90^{}^{\circ}$ and the capacitor voltage lags by $90^{}^{\circ}$. Thus $V_L$ and $V_C$ differ in phase by $180^{}^{\circ}$.

The alternating e.m.f. is the phasor sum:
$E = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$

Substituting the values:
$E = \sqrt{(40)^2 + (20 - 50)^2} = \sqrt{1600 + 900} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\text{ V}$

Final answer: $\boxed{50\text{ V}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inductor of $\left(\frac{100}{\pi}\right) \mathrm{mH}$, capacitor of capacitance $\left(\frac{10^{-3}}{2 \pi}\right) \mathrm{F}$ and resistance of $10 \Omega$ are connected in series with an AC voltage source of $110 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}$ supply. The tangent of the phase angle ' $\phi$ ' between voltage and current is
questions.solution:
The tangent of the phase angle between voltage and current in a series RLC circuit is determined by the inductive and capacitive reactances relative to the resistance.

Given: $R = 10 \Omega$, $L = \frac{100}{\pi} \times 10^{-3} \,\mathrm{H}$, $C = \frac{10^{-3}}{2\pi} \,\mathrm{F}$, and $f = 50 \,\mathrm{Hz}$.

The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi \mathrm{rad/s}$.

Inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = (100\pi) \cdot \left(\frac{100}{\pi} \times 10^{-3}\right) = 10 \,\Omega$.

Capacitive reactance is $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{100\pi \cdot \frac{10^{-3}}{2\pi}} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20 \,\Omega$.

The phase angle satisfies $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R} = \frac{10 - 20}{10} = -1$. Taking the magnitude gives $|\tan\phi| = 1$.

The tangent of the phase angle is $1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a.c. circuit contains resistance of $12 \Omega$ and inductor of inductive reactance $5 \Omega$. The phase angle between current and potential difference will be
questions.solution:
The phase angle $\phi$ between current and potential difference in an AC circuit with resistance $R = 12\,\Omega$ and inductive reactance $X_L = 5\,\Omega$ satisfies $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{5}{12}$.

The impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{144 + 25} = 13\,\Omega$.

From the impedance triangle, $\cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z} = \frac{12}{13}$ and $\sin \phi = \frac{X_L}{Z} = \frac{5}{13}$.

Therefore, $\phi = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{13}\right)$ or equivalently $\phi = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)$.

Comparing with the given options, the correct expression is $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{13}\right)$ which corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an LC circuit, angular frequency at resonance is ' $\omega$ '. What will be the new angular frequency when inductor's inductance is made two times and capacitor's capacitance is made four times?
questions.solution:
The resonant angular frequency of an LC circuit is given by $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

When the inductance is doubled and the capacitance is quadrupled, the new values become $L' = 2L$ and $C' = 4C$.

The new resonant frequency is $\omega' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L'C'}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2L)(4C)}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8LC}}$.

This simplifies to $\omega' = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{\omega}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

The new angular frequency is therefore $\frac{\omega}{2\sqrt{2}}$, which corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An 80 W lamp is connected to the secondary of a step-down transformer, where primary is connected to ac mains of 220 V. Assuming the transformer to be ideal, the current in the primary winding is nearly
questions.solution:
In an ideal transformer, input power equals output power. Given the output power $P_s = 80\text{ W}$ at the lamp and the primary voltage $V_p = 220\text{ V}$, the primary current $I_p$ satisfies $V_p I_p = P_s$.

Substituting the known values, $220 I_p = 80$, so $I_p = \frac{80}{220} = \frac{4}{11}\text{ A} \approx 0.3636\text{ A}$.

Rounded to two decimal places, $I_p \approx 0.36\text{ A}$, which corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resistor of $100 \Omega$, inductor of self inductance $\left(\frac{4}{\pi^2}\right) \mathrm{H}$ and a capacitor of unknown capacitance are connected in series to an a.c. source of $200 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}$ supply. When the current and voltage are in phase, the capacitance and the power dissipated is respectively
questions.solution:
At resonance in an RLC series circuit, the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal: $X_L = X_C$.

The inductive reactance is calculated as $X_L = 2\pi f L = 2\pi (50)\left(\frac{4}{\pi^2}\right) = \frac{400}{\pi} \Omega$.

The resonance condition yields $\frac{400}{\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$, leading to $C = \frac{1}{100 \times 400} = 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{F}$.

At resonance, the impedance equals the resistance $R = 100 \Omega$, so the RMS current is $I_{rms} = \frac{200}{100} = 2 \mathrm{A}$ and the power dissipated is $P = I_{rms}^2 R = 4 \times 100 = 400 \mathrm{W}$.

The capacitance $2.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{F}$ and power $400 \mathrm{W}$ correspond to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The frequency at resonance for the circuit is
questions.solution: For the resonant frequency of the LC circuit, the equivalent inductance for two parallel inductors each L is L _{eq}$=\frac{L}{2}$. The equivalent capacitance for two series capacitors each C is C _{eq}$=\frac{C}{2}$. At resonance, $f=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{eq}C_{eq}}}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{2} \cdot \frac{C}{2}}}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{LC}{4}}}=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{LC}}$. Answer: C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In an a.c. circuit containing $L, C, R$ in series the ratio of true power to apparent power is
( $\mathrm{Z}=$ impedance of the circuit and R is the resistance)
questions.solution:
The true power dissipated in an AC circuit is $P_{\text{true}} = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos\phi$, where $\phi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current.

The apparent power is defined as $P_{\text{apparent}} = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}}$. The ratio gives $\frac{P_{\text{true}}}{P_{\text{apparent}}}} = \cos\phi$, known as the power factor.

In an LCR series circuit, the power factor equals $\frac{R}{Z}$, where $R$ is the resistance and $Z$ is the impedance.

The ratio of true power to apparent power is therefore $\frac{R}{Z}$, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR circuit R $=18 \Omega$ and impedance is $30 \Omega$. An rms voltage 210 V is applied across the circuit. The true power consumed in AC circuit is nearly
questions.solution:
Given a series LCR circuit with resistance $R = 18 \, \Omega$, impedance $Z = 30 \, \Omega$, and RMS voltage $V_{\text{rms}} = 210 \, \text{V}$, the RMS current is determined by Ohm's law:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{210}{30} = 7 \, \text{A}$.

The true power in a resistive component is given by $P = I_{\text{rms}^2 R$, yielding:

$P = (7)^2 \times 18 = 49 \times 18 = 882 \, \text{W}$.

This result is confirmed by the alternative expression $P = \frac{V_{\text{rms}^2 R}{Z^2}$, which evaluates to $\frac{210^2 \times 18}{30^2} = \frac{44100 \times 18}{900} = 882 \, \text{W}$.

The calculated power of $882 \, \text{W}$ is closest to the option $900 \, \text{W}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{900 W}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resistor of $50 \Omega$, inductor of self inductance $\left(\frac{2}{\pi^2}\right) \mathrm{H}$ and a capacitor of unknown capacity are connected in series to an a.c. source of $100 \mathrm{~V}, 50$ Hz supply. When the voltage and current are in phase, the value of capacitance is
questions.solution:
Circuit resonance occurs when voltage and current are in phase in an RLC series circuit, satisfying $X_L = X_C$.

The inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi f L$ and capacitive reactance is $X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$. Setting equal at resonance gives:

$2\pi f L = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$

Solving for capacitance yields $C = \frac{1}{4\pi^2 f^2 L}$.

Substituting given values $R = 50\ \Omega$, $L = \frac{2}{\pi^2}\ \mathrm{H}$, and $f = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$:

$C = \frac{1}{4\pi^2 (50)^2 \left(\frac{2}{\pi^2}\right)} = \frac{1}{4 \times 2500 \times 2} = \frac{1}{20000}\ \mathrm{F}$

Converting to microfarads: $\frac{1}{20000} \times 10^6 = 50\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

This matches option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
L, C and R are connected in series to an a. c. source. Which one of the following is true?
Phase relation between current and voltage is such that
options: both are out of phase with each other in 'R'.
both are in phase in 'L' and out of phase in 'C'.
both are out of phase in ' $L$ ' and in phase in ' $C$ '.
both are out of phase in both 'C' and 'L'.
questions.solution:
Phase relationships in AC circuit elements

For a resistor (R$), voltage and current remain in phase.

In an inductor (L$), voltage leads current by $90^{}^{\circ}$: $V_L$ leads $I$ by $\pi/2$ radians.

For a capacitor (C$), current leads voltage by 90^{}^{\circ}$: $I$ leads $V_C$ by \pi/2$ radians.

Both $L$ and $C$ exhibit 90^{}^{\circ}$ phase differences between voltage and current, making them out of phase in both cases.

The correct statement is $\boxed{D}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR circuit $\mathrm{C}=2 \mu \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{ L}=5 \mathrm{mH}$ and $\mathrm{R}=5 \Omega$. The ratio of energy stored in the inductor to that in capacitor, when maximum current flows through the circuit is
questions.solution:
Given: Series LCR circuit
\(C=2 \mu \mathrm{ F}, \quad L=5 \mathrm{mH}, \quad R=5 \Omega\)
We are asked for the ratio of energy in inductor to that in capacitor when the current through the circuit is maximum → this happens at resonance.
At resonance:
- Impedance \(Z=R\)
- Let supply voltage be \(V\) and current be \(I\). Then
\(V=I R\)
Energy stored in the inductor:
\(U_L=\frac{1}{2}L I²\)
Energy stored in the capacitor (using \(V=I R\) ):
\(U_C=\frac{1}{2}C V²=\frac{1}{2}C(I R)^2\)
Hence,
\(\frac{U_L}{U_C}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} L I^2}{\frac{1}{2} C I^2 R^2}=\frac{L}{C R^2}\)
Substitute values:
\begin{gathered}$\frac{U_L}{U_C}=\frac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 25}=\frac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-5}}=100 \\
\frac{U_L}{U_C}=100: 1
\end{gathered}\)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an $L R$ circuit, the value of $L$ is $\left(\frac{0 \cdot 3}{\pi}\right)$ henry and the value of $R$ is $40 \Omega$, If in the circuit, an alternating e.m.f of 230 V at 50 cycles per second is connected, the impedance of the circuit and current will be respectively
questions.solution:
Impedance and current calculation for LR circuit:

Given $L = \frac{0.3}{\pi}$ H, $R = 40\, \Omega$, $V_{\text{rms}} = 230$ V, and $f = 50$ Hz.
The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi$ rad/s.

The inductive reactance becomes $X_L = \omega L = 100\pi \cdot \frac{0.3}{\pi} = 30\, \Omega$.

The circuit impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\, \Omega$.

Applying Ohm's law yields the current $I = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{230}{50} = 4.6$ A.

These results correspond to option $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an a.c. circuit, a resistance ' $R$ ' is connected in series with an inductance ' $L$ '. If phase angle between voltage and current is $45^{{}^{\circ}}$, the value of inductive reactance will be $\left(\tan 45^{{}^{\circ}}=1\right)$
questions.solution:
In a series $RL$ circuit, the phase angle $\phi$ satisfies $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R}$.

Given $\phi = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$ and $\tan 45^{{}^{\circ}} = 1$, it follows that $1 = \frac{X_L}{R}$.

Multiplying both sides by $R$ yields $X_L = R$, indicating the inductive reactance equals the resistance.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a.c. source of frequency ' $f$ ' is connected to a circuit containing an inductance ' $L$ ' and resistance ' $R$ ' in series. The impedance of this circuit is
questions.solution:
Inductive reactance $X_L$ depends on angular frequency $\omega$ and inductance $L$, with $X_L = \omega L$. Given $\omega = 2\pi f$, it follows that $X_L = 2\pi f L$.

In a series RL circuit, the impedance $Z$ is the phasor sum of resistance $R$ and inductive reactance $X_L$, yielding $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

Substituting for $X_L$ provides $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (2\pi f L)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + 4\pi^2 f^2 L^2}$.

The derived expression corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The reactance of a capacitor is $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}$. If the frequency and the capacitance are doubled, then the new reactance will be
questions.solution:
The capacitive reactance is defined by $X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$.

When both frequency and capacitance are doubled, the new reactance becomes $X_{C2} = \frac{1}{2\pi (2f) (2C)} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{X_C}{4}$.

Final answer: $\frac{X_C}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a. c. voltage is applied to pure inductor. The current in the inductor
questions.solution:
For a pure inductor with inductance $L$ connected to an AC voltage source $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the inductor voltage is $V_L = L \frac{dI}{dt}$.

Equating the applied voltage and inductor voltage gives:

$V_0 \sin(\omega t) = L \frac{dI}{dt}$

Solving for the current by integration:

$dI = \frac{V_0}{L} \sin(\omega t) dt$

$I = \frac{V_0}{L} \int \sin(\omega t) dt = \frac{V_0}{L} \left( -\frac{\cos(\omega t)}{\omega} \right) = -\frac{V_0}{\omega L} \cos(\omega t)$

Using the identity $-\cos\theta = \sin(\theta - \frac{\pi}{2})$, the current becomes:

$I = \frac{V_0}{\omega L} \sin(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2})$

Letting $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\omega L}$ denote the peak current:

$I = I_0 \sin(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2})$

Comparing with the voltage $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the current lags by a phase angle of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

Final answer: C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $The power factor of a CR circuit is \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, If the frequency of a. c. signal is halved, then the power factor of the circuit will become
questions.solution:
The power factor in a CR circuit is defined as $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$, where $R$ is the resistance and $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2}$ is the impedance with capacitive reactance $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.

Given the initial power factor $\cos\phi_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, we equate:

$\frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_{C1}^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Squaring both sides yields $\frac{R^2}{R^2 + X_{C1}^2} = \frac{1}{2}$, which simplifies to $R^2 = X_{C1}^2$. Therefore $R = X_{C1}$.

When the frequency is halved, $f' = f/2$, so the new reactance becomes $X_{C2} = \frac{1}{2\pi f' C} = \frac{1}{2\pi (f/2) C} = 2X_{C1} = 2R$.

The new power factor is:

$\cos\phi_2 = \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_{C2}^2}} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + (2R)^2}} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{5R^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$

The power factor becomes $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In LCR series circuit, when ' $L$ ' is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between voltage and current in the circuit is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. If ' $C$ ' is removed from the circuit instead of $L$ then phase difference is again $\frac{\pi}{3}$. The power factor of the circuit is $\left(\tan 60^{{}^{\circ}}=\sqrt{3}\right)$
questions.solution:
Removing the inductor yields an RC series circuit with phase difference $\phi_1 = \frac{\pi}{3}$, where $\tan \phi_1 = \frac{X_C}{R}$.

Given $\tan \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = \sqrt{3}$, it follows that $\frac{X_C}{R} = \sqrt{3}$.

Removing the capacitor yields an RL series circuit with phase difference $\phi_2 = \frac{\pi}{3}$, where $\tan \phi_2 = \frac{X_L}{R}$.

Since $\tan \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = \sqrt{3}$, we have $\frac{X_L}{R} = \sqrt{3}$.

Combining these results gives $X_C = \sqrt{3} R$ and $X_L = \sqrt{3} R$, implying $X_L = X_C$.

For the original LCR circuit, the phase difference follows $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

Substituting $X_L - X_C = 0$ yields $\tan \phi = 0$, so $\phi = 0$.

The power factor is $\cos \phi = \cos 0 = 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the power factor changes from 0.5 to 0.25 because impedance changes from $Z_1$ to $Z_2$ then $Z_1=x Z_2$. The value of $x$ is (Resistance remains constant)
questions.solution:
The power factor cosφ relates resistance R to impedance Z through $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$, which rearranges to $Z = \frac{R}{\cos\phi}$.

Given $\cos\phi_1 = 0.5$ and $\cos\phi_2 = 0.25$ with constant resistance, the impedances are $Z_1 = \frac{R}{0.5}$ and $Z_2 = \frac{R}{0.25}$.

Substituting $Z_1 = xZ_2$ yields $\frac{R}{0.5} = x \left(\frac{R}{0.25}\right).
Canceling R and simplifying gives $ x = $\frac{0.25}{0.5} =0.5$.

The final answer is B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Same current is flowing in two different a.c. circuits. First circuit contains only inductance and second contains only capacitance. If the frequency of a.c. is increased in both circuits, the current will
options: increase in the first circuit and decrease in second.
decrease in first circuit and increase in second.
questions.solution:
The behavior of current with changing frequency depends on the circuit's reactive components.

For a purely inductive circuit, the inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi fL$. Applying Ohm's law, the current becomes $I_L = V/X_L = V/(2\pi fL)$. Since $f$ appears in the denominator, increasing the frequency causes the current to decrease.

For a purely capacitive circuit, the capacitive reactance is $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$. The current is $I_C = V/X_C = 2\pi fCV$. Here, current increases proportionally with frequency.

The analysis shows that increasing AC frequency decreases current in the inductive circuit while increasing current in the capacitive circuit.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a. c. source is connected across a pure inductor. Which one of the following figures shows the correct phase relation between the current and e.m.f.?
questions.solution:
In an ideal inductor driven by an alternating current source, the voltage leads the current by a phase difference of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radians (or $90^\circ$), or equivalently, the current lags the voltage by $90^\circ$.

Analysis by elimination:

Option (A) depicts a $180^\circ$ phase shift, which is incorrect.
Option (B) shows the voltage along the positive x-axis and the current along the negative y-axis; hence, voltage leads current by $90^\circ$.
Option (C) shows zero phase difference, characteristic of a resistive circuit.
Option (D) illustrates current leading voltage by $90^\circ$, typical of a capacitive circuit.

Only option (B) correctly represents the phase relationship for a pure inductor.

The correct choice is $\boxed{B}$.
questions.question: An a. c. source is connected across a pure inductor. Which one of the following figures shows the correct phase relation between the current and e.m.f.?
questions.explanation:
In an ideal inductor driven by an alternating current source, the voltage leads the current by a phase difference of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radians (or $90^\circ$), or equivalently, the current lags the voltage by $90^\circ$.

Analysis by elimination:

Option (A) depicts a $180^\circ$ phase shift, which is incorrect.
Option (B) shows the voltage along the positive x-axis and the current along the negative y-axis; hence, voltage leads current by $90^\circ$.
Option (C) shows zero phase difference, characteristic of a resistive circuit.
Option (D) illustrates current leading voltage by $90^\circ$, typical of a capacitive circuit.

Only option (B) correctly represents the phase relationship for a pure inductor.

The correct choice is $\boxed{B}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an a.c. circuit with pure capacitance 'C' and a.c. source $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{E}_0 \sin \omega \mathrm{t}$, the equation of instantaneous current is given by
questions.solution:
The instantaneous current in a pure capacitor relates to the voltage by $I = C \frac{dE}{dt}$.

Given $E = E_0 \sin \omega t$, differentiating yields $\frac{dE}{dt} = E_0 \omega \cos \omega t$.

Substituting into the current equation gives $I = C E_0 \omega \cos \omega t$.

Using the identity $\cos \theta = \sin (\theta + \frac{\pi}{2})$, this becomes $I = E_0 \omega C \sin (\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2})$.

This corresponds to option B, with the correct peak current magnitude $E_0 \omega C$ and phase shift $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current of 5 A is flowing at 220 V in a primary coil of a transformer. If the voltage produced in the secondary coil is 2200 V and $50 \%$ of power is lost, then the current in the secondary coil will be
questions.solution:
The primary power is $P_p = V_p I_p = 220 \times 5 = 1100 \text{ W}$.

With 50% power loss, the secondary power becomes $P_s = 0.50 \times 1100 = 550 \text{ W}$.

Given the secondary voltage $V_s = 2200 \text{ V}$, the secondary current is $I_s = \frac{P_s}{V_s} = \frac{550}{2200} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \text{ A}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Figure shows the combination of inductances and capacitances. Resonant frequency of the L - C circuit is
questions.solution:
Resonant frequency analysis

The series combination of inductors $L$ and $2L$ yields equivalent inductance $L_{eq} = L + 2L = 3L$.

The parallel combination of capacitors $C$ and $2C$ gives equivalent capacitance $C_{eq} = C + 2C = 3C$.

The resonant frequency follows from $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{eq}C_{eq}}}$.

Substituting gives $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{9LC}} = \frac{1}{6\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

This corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an a.c. circuit containing $L, C$ and $R$ in series, the ratio of apparent power to the true power is (Z and R are the impedance and resistance respectively, $\phi=$ phase angle)
questions.solution:
Apparent power $S$ in an a.C. circuit is $S = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}}$, or equivalently $S = I_{\text{rms}^2 Z$, where $Z$ is the circuit's impedance.

True power $P$ represents the actual power dissipated and is given by $P = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos \phi$, where $\phi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current, or $P = I_{\text{rms}^2 R$, with $R$ being the resistance.

The ratio of apparent to true power is

$\frac{S}{P} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}}}{V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos \phi} = \frac{1}{\cos \phi}$.

Given that the power factor is $\cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z}$, then

$\frac{1}{\cos \phi} = \frac{Z}{R}$.

Alternatively, starting from the current-based expressions:

$\frac{S}{P} = \frac{I_{\text{rms}^2 Z}{I_{\text{rms}^2 R} = \frac{Z}{R}$.

Thus, the ratio is $\frac{Z}{R}$, which corresponds to option D.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An alternating e.m.f. is given by $e=e_0 \sin \omega t$. In how much time the e.m.f. will have half its maximum value, if e starts from zero ?
$\left(\mathrm{T}=\text{ time period, } \sin 30^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{1}{2}\right)$
questions.solution:
The alternating e.m.f. is characterized by $e = e_0 \sin \omega t$.

For $e = \frac{e_0}{2}$, solving $\sin \omega t = \frac{1}{2}$ yields $\omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}$.

Substituting $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ gives $\frac{2\pi}{T} t = \frac{\pi}{6}$, from which $t = \frac{T}{12}$.

The e.m.f. reaches half its maximum at $t = \frac{T}{12}$ from zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil has inductance 2 H. The ratio of its reactance when it is connected first to an a.c. source and then to a d.c. source is
questions.solution:
The inductive reactance is defined as $X_L = \omega L$, where $\omega = 2\pi f$ is the angular frequency. For an AC source ($f_\text{AC} \neq 0$), the reactance is finite: $X_L = 2\pi f_\text{AC} L$.

For DC sources, the frequency is zero ($f_\text{DC} = 0$), yielding $X_L = 2\pi \cdot 0 \cdot L = 0$.

The ratio of reactances is therefore:

$\frac{X_{L_\text{AC}}}{X_{L_\text{DC}}} = \frac{2\pi f_\text{AC} L}{0} = \infty$

As this diverges, the answer is $\boxed{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a capacitor is connected in series LR circuit, the alternating current flowing in the circuit
questions.solution:
The impedance of a series LR circuit is given by $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

When a capacitor is connected in series with the LR circuit, it becomes an LCR circuit. The new impedance is given by $Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

The net reactance of the circuit changes from $X_L$ to $|X_L - X_C|$. Since the capacitive reactance $X_C$ opposes the inductive reactance $X_L$, the net reactance generally decreases.

As a result, the overall impedance of the circuit decreases ($Z_2 \lt Z_1$).

Since the alternating current is inversely proportional to the impedance ($I = \dfrac{V}{Z}$), a decrease in impedance leads to an increase in the current flowing through the circuit.

Answer: increases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When alternating current is passed through L-R series circuit, the power factor is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $R=50 \Omega$, then the value of $L$ is
$\left[\cos \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \quad \sin \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \tan \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right]$
questions.solution:
Given: Resistance $R = 50 \Omega$, power factor $\cos \phi = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

The phase angle satisfies $\phi = \pm\frac{\pi}{6}$, taking $\phi = \frac{\pi}{6}$ as standard.

For an LR circuit, $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R}$. Substituting known values:

$\tan \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{X_L}{50}$

Solving gives $X_L = \frac{50}{\sqrt{3}} \Omega$.

Using $X_L = \omega L$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$:

$L = \frac{50/\sqrt{3}}{2\pi f}$

Assuming a standard frequency of 50 Hz:

$L = \frac{50}{2\pi\sqrt{3} \cdot 50} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{3}}$ Henry

This corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a.c. e.m.f. of peak value 230 V and frequency 50 Hz is connected to a circuit with $\mathrm{R}=11.5 \Omega, \mathrm{ L}=2.5 \mathrm{H}$ and a capacitor all in series. The value of capacitance is ' $C$ ' for the current in the circuit to be maximum. The value of ' $C$ ' and maximum current are respectively (\pi^2=10$ )$
questions.solution:
Maximum current in an RLC series circuit occurs at resonance when $X_L = X_C$, making the impedance purely resistive with $Z = R$ and current $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R}$.

Given $f = 50 \text{Hz}$ and $\pi^2 = 10$, angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 100\pi$ rad/s.

From $\omega L = \frac{1}{\omega C}$, capacitance is $C = \frac{1}{\omega^2 L} = \frac{1}{(100\pi)^2 (2.5)}$.
Substitute $\pi^2 = 10$ to find $C = \frac{1}{1000000 \times 2.5} = \frac{1}{250000} = 4\mu\text{F}$.

Maximum current is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R} = \frac{230}{11.5} = 20\text{A}$.
Thus, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An ideal inductor of $\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\right) \mathrm{H}$ is connected in series with a $300 \Omega$ resistor.
If a $20 \mathrm{~V}, 200 \mathrm{~Hz}$ alternating source is connected across the combination, the phase difference between the voltage and current is
questions.solution:
The phase difference between voltage and current in an RL circuit is determined by the ratio of inductive reactance to resistance. The inductive reactance is given by $X_L = 2\pi f L = 2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot \frac{1}{\pi} = 400\ \Omega$.

The phase angle satisfies $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{400}{300} = \frac{4}{3}$, yielding $\phi = \tan^{-1} \left(\frac{4}{3}\right).$

The calculated phase difference corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An alternating e.m.f. having voltage $V=V_0 \sin \omega t$ is applied to a series L-C-R circuit. Given : $\left|X_L-X_C\right|=R$. The r.m.s. value of potential difference across capacitor will be
questions.solution:
The peak voltage $V_0$ has r.m.s. value $V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$.

Given $|X_L - X_C| = R$, the circuit impedance becomes $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + R^2} = R\sqrt{2}$.

The r.m.s. current is $I_{\text{rms}} = V_{\text{rms}}/Z = (V_0/\sqrt{2})/(R\sqrt{2}) = V_0/(2R)$.

The r.m.s. voltage across the capacitor is $V_{C,\text{rms}} = I_{\text{rms}} X_C = (V_0/(2R))(1/\omega C)$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\frac{V_0}{2R\omega C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an electrical circuit ' R ', ' L ', ' C ' and an a.c. voltage source are all connected in series. When ' $L$ ' is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between the voltage and the current in the circuit is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. If instead 'C' is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\frac{\pi}{3}$. The power factor of the circuit is $\left(\tan \frac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt{3}\right)$
questions.solution:
Case analysis shows the circuit reaches resonance. When inductance $L$ is removed, $\phi_1 = \frac{\pi}{3}$ for the RC circuit gives $\tan \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_C}{R}$, so $X_C = \sqrt{3}R$.

When capacitance $C$ is removed, $\phi_2 = \frac{\pi}{3}$ for the RL circuit gives $\tan \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_L}{R}$, so $X_L = \sqrt{3}R$.

In the original RLC circuit, $X_L = X_C$, so the impedance simplifies to $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{R^2} = R$. The power factor is therefore $\cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z} = 1$.

Power factor: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In series LCR resonant circuit, $R=800 \Omega, C=2 \mu F$ and voltage across resistance is 200 V. The angular frequency is $250 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. At resonance, the voltage across the inductance is
questions.solution:
Given: Series LCR circuit with $R = 800 \Omega$, $C = 2 \times 10^{-6}$ F, $V_R = 200$ V at angular frequency $\omega = 250$ rad/s.

At resonance, impedance becomes purely resistive, so the current is $I = \frac{V_R}{R} = \frac{200}{800} = 0.25$ A.

The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{250 \cdot 2 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-4}} = 2000 \Omega$.

Since $X_L = X_C$ at resonance, the inductive reactance is also $2000 \Omega$.

The voltage across the inductance is therefore $V_L = I \cdot X_L = 0.25 \times 2000 = 500$ V.

The voltage across the inductance at resonance is $500$ V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If maximum energy is stored in a capacitor at $\mathrm{t}=0$ then the time after which, current in the circuit will be maximum is
questions.solution:
The angular frequency of an LC circuit is given by $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

Given $L = 16 \times 10^{-3}$ H and $C = 10 \times 10^{-6}$ F, the product is $LC = 1.6 \times 10^{-7}$ s$^2$.

The angular frequency becomes $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.6 \times 10^{-7}}} = 2500$ rad/s.

At $t=0$, maximum charge on the capacitor implies $Q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega t)$. The current is $I(t) = -\frac{dQ}{dt} = Q_0 \omega \sin(\omega t)$, which reaches its maximum magnitude when $\sin(\omega t) = \pm 1$.

The first maximum occurs at $\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}$, giving $t = \frac{\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{\pi}{5000}$ s.

This corresponds to one-quarter period $T/4$ since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{LC} = 8\pi \times 10^{-4}$ s, yielding $t = 2\pi \times 10^{-4}$ s.

The correct choice is C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In LCR series circuit, $\mathrm{R}=18 \Omega$ and impedance $33 \Omega$. An r.m.s. voltage of 220 V is applied across the circuit. The true power consumed in a.c. circuit is
questions.solution:
Given: Resistance $R = 18\ \Omega$, impedance $Z = 33\ \Omega$, and RMS voltage $V_{\text{rms}} = 220\ \Omega$.

True power in an AC circuit is given by $P = I_{\text{rms}^2 R$, where $I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z}$.

Substituting values yields:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{220}{33} = \frac{20}{3}\ \Omega$

Then,

$P = \left(\frac{20}{3}\right)^2 \times 18 = \frac{400}{9} \times 18 = 400 \times 2 = 800\ \text{W}$

Alternatively, using power factor $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$ in $P = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos\phi$ leads to the equivalent formula:

$P = \frac{V_{\text{rms}^2 R}{Z^2} = \frac{220^2 \times 18}{33^2} = \frac{400 \times 18}{9} = 800\ \text{W}$

Thus, the true power consumed is $800\ \text{W}$, corresponding to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The reading of the ammeter in the following circuit is
questions.solution:
In this series RLC circuit, the RMS source voltage is the phasor sum of the component voltages: $V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$.

Given $V_L = V_C = 100\text{ V}$ and $V_{rms} = 300\text{ V}$, the expression simplifies to $300 = \sqrt{V_R^2 + 0^2}$, yielding $V_R = 300\text{ V}$.

The RMS current is then determined from Ohm's law: $I_{rms} = \frac{V_R}{R} = \frac{300}{50} = 6\text{ A}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{6\text{ A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a.c. e.m.f. of peak value $=230 \mathrm{ V}$ and frequency 50 Hz is connected to a circuit with $\mathrm{R}=11.5 \Omega, \mathrm{ L}=2.5 \mathrm{H}$ and a capacitor all in series. The value of capacitance is ' C ' for the current in the circuit to be maximum. The value of C and maximum current are respectively (\pi^2=10$ )$
questions.solution:
Resonance condition: Maximum current occurs when $X_L = X_C$, where $\omega L = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.

Angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi(50) = 100\pi\ \text{rad/s}$.

Solving for capacitance: $C = \frac{1}{\omega^2 L} = \frac{1}{(100\pi)^2(2.5)}$.

Using $\pi^2 = 10$: $C = \frac{1}{10000 \cdot 10 \cdot 2.5} = \frac{1}{250000} = 4 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F} = 4\ \mu\text{F}$.

At resonance, impedance equals resistance $Z = R = 11.5\ \Omega$, so peak current $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R} = \frac{230}{11.5} = 20\ \text{A}$.

These values correspond to option B: $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An e.m.f. $\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{E}_0 \cos \omega \mathrm{t}$ is applied to a circuit containing $\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{C}$ and R in series where $X_L=3 R$ and $X_C=R$. The average power dissipated in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The average power dissipated is determined by the power dissipated in the resistor. For a sinusoidal AC source $e = E_{0} \cos \omega t$, the average power is $P_{\text{avg}} = I_{\text{rms}^{2} R$.

The RMS voltage is $V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$. The impedance $Z$ is computed from the resistances: $Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + (3R - R)^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + (2R)^{2}} = \sqrt{5R^{2}} = R\sqrt{5}$.

The RMS current follows as $I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2} R\sqrt{5}} = \frac{E_{0}}{R\sqrt{10}}$.

Substituting into the power formula:

$P_{\text{avg}} = \left( \frac{E_{0}}{R\sqrt{10}} \right)^{2} R = \frac{E_{0}^{2}}{R^{2} \cdot 10} R = \frac{E_{0}^{2}}{10R}$.

Final answer: $\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{10R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal transformer converts 220 a.c. to 3.3 kV a.c. to transmit a power of 4.4 kW. If primary coil has 600 turns then alternating current in secondary coil is
questions.solution:
Alternating Current in Secondary Coil

For an ideal transformer, power is conserved between the primary and secondary coils.

The power supplied to the primary equals the power delivered by the secondary:

$P = V_s I_s$

Substitute $P = 4400 \text{W}$ and $V_s = 3300 \text{V}$:

$4400 = 3300 I_s$

Solving for $I_s$:

$I_s = \frac{4400}{3300} = \frac{44}{33} = \frac{4}{3} \text{A}$

This corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $20 \Omega$ resistance, 10 mH inductance coil and $15 \mu \mathrm{ F}$ capacitor are joined in series. When a suitable frequency alternating current source is joined to this combination, the circuit resonates. If the resistance is made $\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{rd}$, the resonant frequency
questions.solution:
Resonant frequency for a series RLC circuit is defined by the expression $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

This formulation explicitly demonstrates that $f_0$ is a function solely of the inductance $L$ and capacitance $C$. Since resistance $R$ does not appear in the equation, altering $R$ to $\frac{1}{3}$ of its original value has no effect.

The resonant frequency remains unchanged.

Correct option: A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A resistance of $200 \Omega$ and an inductor of $\frac{1}{2 \pi} \mathrm{H}$ are connected in series to a.c. voltage of 40 V and 100 Hz frequency. The phase angle between the voltage and current is
questions.solution:
The inductive reactance is determined using the formula $X_L = 2\pi f L$.

Given $L = \frac{1}{2\pi}\ \mathrm{H}$ and $f = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}$, the computation simplifies to $X_L = 2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi} = 100\ \Omega$.

The phase angle $\phi$ between voltage and current follows from the relation $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R}$.

With $R = 200\ \Omega$ and $X_L = 100\ \Omega$, this yields $\tan \phi = \frac{100}{200} = 0.5$.

The phase angle is therefore $\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.5)$, corresponding to option D.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of resistance $450 \Omega$ and self - inductance 1.5 henry is connected to an a.c. source of frequency $\frac{150}{\pi} \mathrm{ Hz}$. The phase difference between voltage and current is
questions.solution:
Phase difference in RL circuit

The phase angle $\phi$ between voltage and current satisfies $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R}$, where $X_L$ is inductive reactance and $R$ is resistance.

Given $R = 450\ \Omega$, $L = 1.5\ \text{H}$, and $f = \frac{150}{\pi}\ \text{Hz}$, the inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi f L = 2\pi \cdot \frac{150}{\pi} \cdot 1.5 = 450\ \Omega$.

Substituting into the phase formula: $\tan \phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{450}{450} = 1$.

The phase difference is therefore $\phi = \tan^{-1}(1)$, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an $L-R$ circuit, the inductive reactance is equal to $\sqrt{3} times the resistance ' $R$ ' of the circuit. An e.m.f. $E=E_0 \sin (\omega t)$ is applied to the circuit. The power consumed in the circuit is$
questions.solution:
Inductive reactance is given as $X_L = \sqrt{3} R$.

For an L-R circuit, the impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$. Substituting the given reactance yields:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\sqrt{3} R)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + 3R^2} = \sqrt{4R^2} = 2R$

The RMS voltage is $E_{\text{rms}} = E_0/\sqrt{2}$, so the RMS current becomes:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2} \cdot 2R} = \frac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}R}$

The power factor is $\cos\phi = R/Z = R/(2R) = 1/2$.
Power consumption follows $P = E_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos\phi$:

$P = \left(\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \left(\frac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}R}\right) \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{E_0^2}{8R}$

Verifying with $P = I_{\text{rms}^2 R$ gives the same result:
$P = \left(\frac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}R}\right)^2 R = \frac{E_0^2}{8R}$

The power consumed is therefore $\frac{E_0^2}{8R}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An a.c. source is applied to a series LR circuit with $X_L=3 R$ and power factor is $X_1$. Now a capacitor with $X_C=R$ is added in series to LR circuit and the power factor is $X_2$. The ratio $X_1$ to $X_2$ is
questions.solution:
The ratio of power factors $X_1$ to $X_2$ is determined by comparing the impedance characteristics of two circuits.

For the series LR circuit with $X_L = 3R$, the impedance is $Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + (3R)^2} = R\sqrt{10}$. The power factor is then $X_1 = \frac{R}{Z_1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$.

For the series LCR circuit with $X_L = 3R$ and $X_C = R$, the impedance becomes $Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (3R - R)^2} = R\sqrt{5}$. This yields a power factor of $X_2 = \frac{R}{Z_2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

The desired ratio is $\frac{X_1}{X_2} = \frac{1/\sqrt{10}}{1/\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{10}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, corresponding to a ratio of $1 : \sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series LCR circuit is connected to an a.c. source of $230 \mathrm{ V}, 50 \mathrm{ Hz}$. The circuit contains resistance of $80 \Omega$ an inductor having inductive reactance $70 \Omega$ and a capacitor of capacitive reactance $130 \Omega$. The power factor of the circuit is $x$. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
The power factor of a series LCR circuit is determined by the ratio of resistance to impedance.

Given resistance $R = 80\ \Omega$, inductive reactance $X_L = 70\ \Omega$, and capacitive reactance $X_C = 130\ \Omega$, the net reactance is $X = X_C - X_L = 60\ \Omega$ since $X_C > X_L$.

The impedance follows as $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2} = \sqrt{80^2 + 60^2} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\ \Omega$.

Thus, the power factor is $\cos \phi = R/Z = 80/100 = 0.8$.

This corresponds to option B, so the answer is $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An alternating voltage $\mathrm{E}=100 \sqrt{2} \sin (50 \mathrm{t})$ is connected to a $2 \mu \mathrm{F}$ capacitor through an a.c. ammeter. The ammeter reading will be
questions.solution:
The alternating voltage is given by $E = 100 \sqrt{2} \sin(50t)$, corresponding to a peak voltage $E_0 = 100 \sqrt{2} \text{ V}$ and angular frequency $\omega = 50 \text{ rad/s}$.

For the capacitor with capacitance $C = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$, the capacitive reactance is $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{50 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}} = 10^4 \ \Omega$.

The peak current is $I_0 = \frac{E_0}{X_C} = \frac{100 \sqrt{2}}{10^4} = 0.01 \sqrt{2} \text{ A}$.

Since the ammeter measures the RMS current, we compute $I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{0.01 \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.01 \text{ A}$. Converting to milliamperes gives $I_{\text{rms}} = 10 \text{ mA}$.

The ammeter reading is $\boxed{\text{10 mA}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The instantaneous value of current in an a.c. circuit is $I=3 \sin\left(50 \pi t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \mathrm{A}$. The current will be maximum for the first time at
questions.solution: The current is expressed as $I = 3 \sin \left(50\pi$ t + $\frac{\pi}{4}\right) amperes. The maximum of the sine function occurs when its argument is \frac{\pi}{2}.Set 50\pi$ t + $\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2} and solve for $ t$:50\pi$ t = $\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4}Dividing both sides by \pi gives 50t = \frac{1}{4}.Thus, $ t = $\frac{1}{4 \times 50} = \frac{1}{200} seconds, matching option C.$

questions.q: An inductance of 2 mH , a condenser of $20 \mu \mathrm{ F}$ and a resistance of $50 \Omega$ are connected in series to an a.c. source. The reactance of inductor and condenser are same. The reactance of either of them will be

questions.q: A light bulb connected in series with a capacitor and an a.c. source is glowing with a certain brightness. On reducing the capacity of capacitance and frequency of source, the brightness of the lamp (respectively)
questions.solution: The capacitive reactance is given by $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{2 \pi \mathrm{fC}}$ If f or C is reduced, $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}$ will also increase. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Average power associated with an ideal inductor and ideal capacitor over a complete cycle of a.c. is respectively
questions.solution:
1. Ideal Inductor:
- The voltage and current in an ideal inductor are out of phase by 90 degrees, with the current lagging the voltage by $90^{{}^{\circ}}$.
- The instantaneous power is given by $p(t)=v(t) \times i(t)$.
- Over a complete cycle, the positive and negative power values cancel out, resulting in an average power of zero.
2. Ideal Capacitor:
- In an ideal capacitor, the voltage and current are also out of phase by 90 degrees, but this time, the current leads the voltage by $90^{{}^{\circ}}$.
- Similar to the inductor case, the instantaneous power alternates between positive and negative, resulting in an average power of zero over a complete cycle.

questions.solution:

$\begin{aligned}

& \therefore \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\omega \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
& \therefore \quad\left(\frac{\omega \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2+1=2 \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\omega \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}}=1
\end{aligned}$
So, when the AC frequency is doubled,
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\omega \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}} & =2 \\
\therefore \quad \cos \phi & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\omega \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(2)^2}} \\
\therefore \quad \cos \phi & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A circuit containing resistance $\mathrm{R}_1$, inductance $\mathrm{L}_1$ and capacitance $\mathrm{C}_1$ connected in series resonates at the same frequency ' $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{r}}$ ' as another circuit containing $\mathrm{R}_2, \mathrm{ L}_2$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ in series. If two circuits are connected in series, then the new frequency at resonance is
questions.solution:
When $\mathrm{R}_1, \mathrm{~L}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_1$ are connected in series the resonant (angular) frequency is given by
$$
\omega_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{L}_1 \cdot \mathrm{C}_1}}
$$
Also, when $\mathrm{R}_2, \mathrm{~L}_2, \mathrm{C}_2$ are connected in series
Then $\omega_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{L}_2 \cdot \mathrm{C}_2}}$
By (1) and (2): $\mathrm{L}_1 \mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_2$
If the two circuits are connected in series then the equivalent inductance is given by $\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L}_1+\mathrm{L}_2$ and the equivalent capacitance is given by
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{C}=\frac{\mathrm{C}_1 \mathrm{C}_2}{\mathrm{C}_1+\mathrm{C}_2} \\
& \therefore \mathrm{LC}=\left(\mathrm{L}_1+\mathrm{L}_2\right) \cdot \frac{\mathrm{C}_1 \mathrm{C}_2}{\mathrm{C}_1+\mathrm{C}_2} \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{L}_1 \mathrm{C}_1 \mathrm{C}_2+\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_1 \mathrm{C}_2}{\mathrm{C}_1+\mathrm{C}_2}\left[\because \mathrm{L}_1 \mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_2\right] \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_2\left(\mathrm{C}_2+\mathrm{C}_1\right)}{\mathrm{C}_1+\mathrm{C}_2}=\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_2 \\
& \therefore \omega=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{L}_2 \mathrm{C}_2}}=\omega_{\mathrm{r}}
\end{aligned}
$$
